questions.title: Design async RL rollout and control the sample age
questions.prompt: You move an RL job from one GPU to a cluster where the rollout engines and the trainers run on separate devices. The team wants generation and training to run at the same time, so that neither side waits for the other. Design the async setup: which knobs matter, what new failure appears, and what you watch in the logs.
questions.short: Async training lets the engines generate the next batch while the trainer updates, at the price of samples that come from older weights. Two modes exist: one step ahead, where every sample is at most one weight version old with the default update interval, and fully async, where a worker keeps generating and the trainer drains a buffer, so the age depends on how fast the trainer drains it. Set a limit on sample age, decide what happens to running requests at each weight update, and lower the learning rate as you allow older samples. Watch the weight version of each sample, the share of dropped samples, the clip fraction, and the gap between the two sides.
questions.full:
### Why async pays off only on a split layout

With both sides on one GPU they take turns, and generation stops for the whole training window; the colocated fully async mode exists only to learn the settings. On separate devices the trainer idles during rollout and the engines idle during training unless the two overlap. Async removes part of that wait.

### The knobs

| Setting | What it decides |
|---|---|
| `--update-weights-interval` | how many steps run between weight updates to the engines |
| `--max-weight-staleness` | the oldest weight version a sample may come from; unset means no limit |
| `--async-unused-samples-handler` | drop or retry a sample that is too old |
| `--async-max-concurrent-samples` | how many samples the engines generate at one time |
| `--pause-generation-mode` | what happens to running requests at a weight update: abort, retract, or in place; retract is the default |

The over-sampling batch size has no effect in the fully async mode.

### The new failure: stale samples

A sample generated under weights two versions old is off-policy for the trainer. The ratio of trainer probability to engine probability now carries a gap that the kernels did not cause. Two signals show it. The clip fraction, `train/pg_clipfrac`, is 0 in a run with one optimizer update per rollout, because the policy that trains is the one that sampled; a clip fraction above 0 in such a run means the samples did not come from the current weights. The log-probability gap grows with the age for the same reason.

### Learning rate follows age

A study of asynchronous GRPO on small models changed the steps between weight updates and the learning rate together, and the largest stable learning rate fell in proportion to the steps between updates: twice the steps, about half the rate. The manual has not tested it and offers it as the starting rule. When you raise the update interval or the age limit, lower the learning rate by the same factor, then watch the gap and the reward.

### What to watch

- The weight version statistics in the rollout metrics: how old the samples are.
- The share of dropped or retried samples. A high share means the engines work for nothing.
- `train/pg_clipfrac` and the gap, read against the ranges of your synchronous runs.
- `perf/update_weights_time` against the step time. On a split layout the update is a transfer over the network, not a copy inside one GPU, and the transfer method is a choice of its own.

### Corrections for what remains

A sample age limit drops the worst samples. For the rest, the truncated importance-sampling correction reweights each token by the ratio of the two probabilities with a cap. Remove staleness before you reweight it.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** Why is the clip fraction exactly 0 in a synchronous run with one update per rollout? Expected: the policy in the trainer is still the policy that produced the samples, so every ratio is 1 and nothing hits the clip range.
- **Level 4:** Which pause mode do you choose, and what does the wrong one cost? Expected: retract keeps the work of running requests and continues them under new weights, which mixes weight versions inside one answer; abort throws the work away; in place changes the weights under a running request; the fully async mode refuses some of these, so read the flag help of your version.
- **Level 4:** A partial answer started under version 5 and finished under version 7. Where does that show up? Expected: in the gap, because part of its tokens come from older weights than the trainer holds; watch the gap after you turn on partial rollout or raise the staleness limit.
- **Level 4:** How does a dedicated evaluation fleet fit this design? Expected: it loads checkpoint snapshots and never takes part in the training weight updates, so its lag is reported in steps; in the version the manual read it does not combine with rollout fault tolerance.
questions.wrong:
- "Run fully async on the single GPU too; it is the same code." With one GPU the two sides still take turns and generation stops during training, so you pay the staleness cost and get no overlap.
- "Leave the staleness limit unset, so that no sample is wasted." Unset means no limit; very old samples pull the update in the wrong direction, and the gap grows without a cause in the kernels.
- "Keep the learning rate from the synchronous run." The stable rate falls with the age of the samples; raise the update interval and you lower the rate by about the same factor.

questions.title: Train the head only, or fine-tune the whole model
questions.prompt: You have a small pretrained transformer and 800 labelled text messages, half of them spam. You need a binary classifier by tomorrow. Do you train only a new classification head, or do you update every weight? Defend the choice.
questions.short: Swap the language-model head for a two-class linear layer and start with the body frozen. Head-only training is fast, costs almost no memory, and rarely overfits on this little data. Unfreeze the body only when the frozen run leaves accuracy on the table and the domain is far from the pretraining text.
questions.full:
### Two regimes, one loop

The body maps tokens to hidden states and stays as it is. The head maps a pooled hidden state to two logits and is new. Head-only training sets `requires_grad=False` on the body, so the optimizer sees only the head. Full fine-tuning lets the gradient flow through the whole stack, and the body drifts toward the classification objective.

### What each one buys

On the fixture in the capstone lesson, head-only training reached a precision near 0.9 and a recall near 0.85 after twenty epochs. Full fine-tuning took about three times longer and landed within a couple of points either way, depending on the seed. With 800 examples the body has little to learn from the labels, and a lot to forget.

### Pooling

A classifier needs one vector per sequence. Mean pooling weighted by the attention mask is the simplest choice and gives a stable signal across lengths. A CLS token needs pretraining of that token. Last-token pooling is what decoder-style classifiers use.

### Read the numbers, not one accuracy

Report precision, recall, F1 and the confusion matrix on a held-out split with a known balance. The lesson splits 80/20 into 640 training and 160 test messages, stratified so that the test set keeps its balance.

### When the full update starts to pay

On 80,000 examples and a larger body, the body has enough signal to move without overfitting, and a domain shift can justify the cost. A middle path unfreezes only the last block.
questions.followups:
- **Level 1:** What does `requires_grad=False` on the body do to the optimizer? Expected: the optimizer receives only the head parameters, so the body weights never change.
- **Level 2:** Why mean pooling and not the last hidden state? Expected: mean pooling with the mask is stable across lengths and needs no special token; last-token pooling suits decoder models that saw that pattern.
- **Level 2:** Why keep the test split stratified? Expected: a known class balance lets you read precision and recall as honest numbers.
- **Level 3:** The full update scores lower than the frozen run on this data. What happened? Expected: the body overfit the small set and lost pretrained structure; lower the body learning rate, unfreeze fewer blocks, or stay with the head.
questions.wrong:
- "Train a fresh classifier from scratch, the model is small anyway." The pretrained body already encodes word identity, position and co-occurrence; a new model from 800 examples throws that away.
- "Updating every weight is always more accurate, so do it." On 800 examples it lands within a couple of points of the frozen run and costs about three times the training time, with a real risk of overfitting.
- "Report accuracy, the classes are balanced." Precision and recall tell you which error you make, and the confusion matrix shows the counts behind the score.

questions.title: Replacing the human labeler with a principled model
questions.prompt: Your rater budget is gone. A colleague proposes to replace the human labelers with a model that reads a short list of principles and ranks the pairs, and to run the same RLHF pipeline on those labels. Is this just a cheaper RLHF? What changes?
questions.short: It is the constitutional recipe, and it changes the failure modes rather than removing them. Phase one has the model critique and revise its own answers against sampled principles and trains on the revisions; phase two trains a reward model on pairs ranked by a feedback model and runs the usual RL stage. Rater psychology stops being the bias, and the reading of the principle set becomes the bias, applied uniformly over the whole dataset. Sycophancy toward a rater drops, and the proxy problem stays.
questions.full:
### The two phases

1. Self-critique and revision. Start from a helpful but not yet harmless SFT model. For a red-team prompt, the model writes an answer, a second pass reads one sampled principle and critiques the answer, and a third pass revises it. The revision is the SFT target. The original work used 16 principles and kept the set small so that critiques stay focused.
2. RL from AI feedback. Generate pairs, let a feedback model rank them against sampled principles, train a reward model on those rankings, and run PPO against it. Everything after the label is the standard pipeline.

### Why it is not only cheaper

- The bias moves. A human rater is inconsistent and pleased by agreement; a feedback model applies one reading of a principle to every pair, strict or loose, but uniform.
- The signal is legible. You can read the principle, the critique and the revision for any example; human labels are opaque.
- Goodhart stays. The proxy is now a model's reading of the principle set, still an imperfect measure, so over-optimization against it is still possible.
- The labeler is the same class of model you train, so a bias in it can be amplified rather than averaged out.

### What the original work claimed

The trained model was more harmless and about as helpful as an RLHF model with comparable data. That result has held across labs.

### A gate next to the training

A parallel defense trains light classifiers that read the same principles and gate the outputs. The first version cost 23.7 percent extra compute; the later version about 1 percent. Training shapes behavior and classifiers enforce invariants; neither one is enough alone.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** Why does the recipe sample one principle per critique instead of giving the model the whole list? Expected: a focused critique is more specific and more useful as a training target; the list as a whole is covered over many samples.
- **Level 2:** Which parts of the pipeline change and which stay? Expected: the label source and the SFT targets change; the reward model, the RL stage and the KL penalty stay.
- **Level 3:** Name a sycophancy-like failure that still occurs with an AI labeler, and a check for it. Expected: the feedback model can prefer answers that quote the principles without following them; rate a held-out set with people and compare the two rankings.
- **Level 4:** How do you argue for a priority order among principles? Expected: conflicts between principles need a resolution rule; a tiered order resolves them top-down, from catastrophic harm to platform rules to general ethics to helpfulness.
questions.wrong:
- "The labels are free now, so collect ten times more pairs." More pairs with the same uniform bias make the bias stronger, not weaker; the volume gain does not fix the proxy.
- "An AI labeler removes human bias from alignment." It replaces rater bias with principle-interpretation bias; the principles and the labeler's reading of them are now the proxy.
- "This is only a safety trick; it does not touch helpfulness." The original work reports about the same helpfulness as RLHF with comparable data, and the same critique loop can target any principle you write.

questions.title: Does dropping the reward model end reward hacking
questions.prompt: A staff engineer argues that moving every alignment run from PPO to direct preference methods ends the reward-hacking problem, because there is no reward model left to hack. Make the counter-argument with the mechanism, and say what survives in your pipeline either way.
questions.short: Direct methods remove the explicit reward model, not the proxy. The quantity they optimize is the log ratio of policy to reference, an implicit reward that the preference data pins down only where the data has coverage. Under optimization the policy queries that ratio out of distribution, and the published curves of gold reward against KL show the same peak and then collapse as reward-model pipelines, with the KL regularization failing to stabilize it. What survives: a blind held-out eval, early stopping, broader preference data, and ensembles of signals.
questions.full:
### The mechanism

DPO rewrites the reward as beta times the log ratio of policy to reference. That function is fit from pairs, and it is constrained only on the pairs. Everywhere else its value is whatever the parameterization implies. As the policy moves to raise the margin, it samples from regions no pair covered, where the implicit reward is arbitrary. The study of scaling laws for over-optimization in direct alignment trained policies across KL budgets and found the same shape as reward-model over-optimization: the gold reward rises, peaks, and falls as the KL grows.

### Where Goodhart bites now

In the PPO stack the proxy is a trained reward model. In the direct stack the proxy is the ratio against the reference. The failures look different: the degraded chosen response, where the chosen answer loses probability while the margin grows; length exploitation, where a longer winner pads the gap; arbitrary rewards on pairs that are rare under the reference. They are one disease in a different organ.

### Why the KL does not save it

In PPO the KL term is explicit and tunable, and an adaptive controller holds it near a target. In DPO the anchor is structural: the sigmoid saturates as the ratio grows. The study's result is that this structural regularization does not stop the collapse. Beta changes the speed, not the shape.

### What survives in any pipeline

- A blind, held-out human or trusted-judge eval on a fixed prompt set, read at every checkpoint. It is the one signal the policy cannot game.
- Early stopping on that eval, not on the training margin.
- Data: coverage of the regions the policy drifts into, collected from the current policy's samples.
- Ensembles: several reward signals or several losses on one battery, because one exploit rarely fits all of them.
- Logs of the absolute chosen log-probability and of the KL to the reference, so that the drift is visible before the eval falls.

### The honest version of the claim

Direct methods do remove a model to train and host, PPO's instability, and the class of exploits that live in reward model weights. They are the default for most frontier post-training runs for those reasons. They do not remove the need to guard against over-optimization, so the guard moves into the pipeline design.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** What does DPO remove from the PPO stack, concretely? Expected: a reward model to train and host, the PPO loop with its clip and value head, and an explicit KL coefficient; it keeps the frozen reference.
- **Level 4:** Which variant bounds the gap, and what does that buy against this failure? Expected: the identity-mapping loss, whose margin target is one over two beta; it stops a weak preference from producing an unbounded implicit reward, which removes one path to collapse but not the out-of-distribution query.
- **Level 4:** How do you detect over-optimization without a gold reward? Expected: a held-out eval with generation, the absolute chosen log-probability, the KL to the reference, and a comparison across checkpoints; a margin that grows while the eval falls is the signature.
- **Level 4:** Does iterating, with fresh pairs from the current policy each round, help? Expected: yes, it moves the data coverage to where the policy lives, which is what the reference-ratio proxy lacks; it also reintroduces an online loop that needs its own stop rule.
questions.wrong:
- "No reward model means nothing to hack." The implicit reward is a function the data pins down only on the pairs; the policy can push it anywhere else.
- "The structural KL in DPO is enough regularization." The published curves show the same peak and collapse across KL budgets; beta changes the speed, not the shape.
- "Use a smaller beta so the policy learns faster and you can stop earlier." A smaller beta lets the policy move further from the reference per unit of margin, which is the direction of the failure.

questions.title: Margin up, chosen answers down, in a DPO run
questions.prompt: During a DPO run the loss falls and the reward margin that the trainer logs grows every epoch. Yet the model's samples get shorter and less fluent, and the policy now gives the chosen training answers a lower probability than they had under the reference. Explain the mechanism and what you change.
questions.short: The DPO loss cares only about the difference of two log ratios. It can lower the probability of the chosen answer as long as the rejected answer falls faster, and the margin still grows. This is the degraded chosen response failure: the policy moves probability mass away from both training answers, often toward short degenerate outputs. Log the absolute chosen log-probability, add a penalty on downward moves of the chosen term as the behavior-preserving variant does or switch to a loss with a bounded margin, and keep a generation eval next to the margin.
questions.full:
### Why the margin can lie

The DPO gradient pushes the chosen log ratio up and the rejected log ratio down, but only their difference enters the loss. If the rejected answers are easy to suppress, the cheapest way to grow the margin is to suppress them hard while the chosen answers drift down too. The implicit reward gap is also unbounded: a weak preference can produce an arbitrarily large gap. Nothing in the loss asks the policy to keep generating the chosen answers.

### What you log

- The absolute chosen log-probability under the policy, per epoch, next to the margin. The capstone's margin function reports the difference; add the chosen term alone.
- Sample lengths and a small generation eval. A margin that grows while samples degrade is the signature.
- The KL to the reference. The move away from both answers shows up as a growing distance.

### The fixes

1. A penalty on downward moves of the chosen log-probability. The behavior-preserving variant of the family adds that one correction and reports a gain over plain DPO on reasoning tasks.
2. A bounded margin. The identity-mapping variant replaces the log sigmoid with a squared error on a target of one over two beta, so the gap and the preference strength stay proportional.
3. A conservative beta and early stopping, chosen against a generation eval, not against the training margin.
4. Better pairs. Pairs where both answers are rare under the reference produce arbitrary implicit rewards; filter them.

### Why this is still over-optimization

Direct alignment methods remove the explicit reward model, not the proxy. The quantity they optimize is a ratio against the reference, and that ratio can be pushed to places the preference data never covered. The same peak-and-collapse curve that reward models show appears here across KL budgets.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** Why does length matter in this failure? Expected: a long rejected answer has a more negative total log-probability by construction, so suppressing it is cheap and the gap grows for the wrong reason; length normalization removes that incentive.
- **Level 3:** How does a reference-free, length-normalized loss change the picture? Expected: it scores the average log-probability per token with a margin, which removes the length bias and the reference, but it also removes the anchor, so drift needs its own guard.
- **Level 4:** Which variant do you pick when preference strengths vary widely across pairs? Expected: the bounded one; it keeps the gap proportional to the preference, so strong pairs do not saturate the loss and weak pairs do not blow up.
- **Level 4:** Does a lower beta help here? Expected: no; a lower beta lets the policy move further from the reference for the same margin, which makes the degradation worse.
questions.wrong:
- "The margin grows, so training works; the samples are a decoding problem." The margin can grow while both answers lose probability; the generation eval is the objective, not the margin.
- "Raise beta until the samples recover." A higher beta slows the drift but does not change the direction of the gradient on the chosen term; the penalty on that term does.
- "Train more epochs; the chosen probability will come back." The loss has no term that rewards a higher chosen probability on its own, so more epochs push further the same way.

questions.title: Where the reward model went in DPO
questions.prompt: DPO is often described as RLHF without a reward model. Walk me through where the reward went. Start from the RLHF objective with its KL term and end at the loss you would implement.
questions.short: The penalized objective has a closed-form optimum: the optimal policy equals the reference policy times the exponential of reward over beta, normalized per prompt. Invert it and the reward equals beta times the log ratio of policy to reference, plus a term that depends on the prompt alone. Put that reward into the Bradley-Terry preference probability and the prompt-only term cancels, because both answers share the prompt. What is left is a loss in the policy's own log-probabilities: minus the log sigmoid of beta times the difference of the two log ratios.
questions.full:
### The derivation in four lines

```text
optimum:  pi*(y|x) = pi_ref(y|x) * exp( r(x,y) / beta ) / Z(x)
invert:   r(x,y) = beta * log( pi*(y|x) / pi_ref(y|x) ) + beta * log Z(x)
BT:       P(y_w > y_l | x) = sigmoid( r(x,y_w) - r(x,y_l) )
loss:     -log sigmoid( beta * [ log pi(y_w|x)/pi_ref(y_w|x) - log pi(y_l|x)/pi_ref(y_l|x) ] )
```

The log Z term depends on the prompt alone, so it is the same for the chosen and the rejected answer and drops out of the difference.

### What you compute per pair

Four sequence log-probabilities: the policy and the reference on the chosen answer, and both on the rejected answer. Each is the sum of next-token log-probabilities over the answer tokens only, with the prompt positions masked. The reference runs under no gradient.

### The implicit reward

`beta * (log pi(y|x) - log pi_ref(y|x))` is the reward that DPO assigns to an answer. Log the margin between the chosen and the rejected implicit rewards; it should grow during training. The gradient on the chosen log-probability is `-beta * (1 - sigmoid(z))`, negative for every z, so training pushes the chosen answer up and the rejected answer down.

### Where the KL went

No KL term appears in the loss. The constraint is structural: a large move from the reference makes the log ratio large, the sigmoid saturates, and the gradient fades. Beta sets how far the policy may move. The DPO lesson gives 0.1 to 0.5 as the range and 0.1 to 0.3 as the usual sweet spot. A small beta allows large moves and risks degenerate answers; a value near 1.0 pins the policy to the reference.

### What it saves

Two models in memory instead of three or four, and one supervised loop instead of PPO. For a 70B model each copy takes 140GB in FP16, so the reward model you never load is a large saving.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** Why must the policy start as a copy of the reference? Expected: the derivation treats the optimum as the reference plus a learned shift, and a copy makes every implicit reward start at zero.
- **Level 2:** What does a positive log ratio mean? Expected: the policy now gives that answer a higher probability than the reference does.
- **Level 3:** Why does the derivation need both answers to share one prompt? Expected: the partition term depends on the prompt only; with different prompts it would not cancel, and the implicit rewards would not be comparable.
- **Level 4:** Which assumptions of the derivation fail in practice? Expected: that the optimum is reachable, that the pairs are in-distribution for the reference, and that the reference is the true anchor; each later method in the family repairs one of them.
questions.wrong:
- "DPO has no reference model, that is the point." It removes the reward model and PPO; the frozen reference stays in the loss, and the methods that drop it are a later variant.
- "DPO maximizes the probability of the chosen answer." It maximizes the margin of two log ratios; the chosen absolute probability can fall as long as the rejected falls faster.
- "Beta is a learning rate." Beta scales the implicit reward and sets how far the policy may move from the reference; the optimizer step size is a separate setting.

questions.title: DPO or the full RLHF stack for a small team
questions.prompt: A team of four engineers with eight GPUs has about 20,000 preference pairs for a customer support assistant and wants it aligned in three weeks. One engineer wants the full RLHF stack with a reward model and PPO. Another wants DPO. Which do you pick, and under what conditions would you reverse the choice?
questions.short: Pick DPO. With tens of thousands of pairs it matches or beats the full stack, it trains one model against a frozen reference in a supervised loop, it needs about a third of the compute, and each experiment takes hours instead of days. Reverse the choice when the signal has several dimensions and needs a learned reward you can inspect and reuse, when you want an online loop that rates fresh samples, or when DPO plateaus on your eval.
questions.full:
### What DPO buys

| Aspect | RLHF with PPO | DPO |
|---|---|---|
| Models trained | three: SFT, reward, policy | one: the policy |
| Models in memory | three or four during PPO | two: policy and reference |
| Hyperparameters | learning rate, KL coefficient, clip ratio, reward model rate, epochs for each stage | learning rate, beta, epochs |
| Stability | sensitive to the settings | close to SFT |

For a 70B model each copy takes 140GB in FP16, so one model fewer in memory is a different hardware tier.

### When DPO wins

- Small datasets, 5,000 to 20,000 pairs. A reward model needs enough data to generalize and overfits below that; DPO never fits one.
- Limited compute. One training loop instead of three, roughly one third of the full stack.
- Fast iteration. Trying 10 preference sets takes ten runs of hours each, with no reward model to retrain for each one.

The lesson's reference result: a 7B model aligned with DPO on 60K pairs scored 6.47 on a chat benchmark against 6.86 for a 70B chat model trained with the full stack, within six percent of a model ten times its size.

### When the full stack wins

- Several quality dimensions at once, such as helpfulness, harmlessness and honesty. A reward model learns the trade-off; DPO sees each pair as one binary signal.
- An online loop: sample from the current policy, rate, retrain the reward model, continue. DPO works on a fixed set.
- A reward model you can reuse for best-of-N sampling or as a judge at decode time.
- The largest scales, where a separate reward model has captured more nuance in published pipelines.

### The practical path

Start with DPO. Switch to the full stack when the eval plateaus. Several production pipelines run both: the full stack first for broad alignment, DPO after it for targeted refinement.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** What does the DPO run still need from the RLHF recipe? Expected: an SFT checkpoint as the frozen reference, a held-out eval, and a beta choice that plays the role of the KL coefficient.
- **Level 3:** The pairs come from an older model's outputs. Does that matter for DPO? Expected: yes; pairs that are rare under the reference produce arbitrary implicit rewards, so sample the pairs from the SFT model or filter them by reference likelihood.
- **Level 4:** How would you turn the three weeks into an iterative loop without PPO? Expected: run DPO, generate from the new policy, collect preferences on those samples, run DPO again; the lesson's exercise calls this iterative DPO.
- **Level 4:** Which failure mode do both methods share? Expected: over-optimization of a proxy, the reward model in one case and the ratio to the reference in the other; both need a blind eval and early stopping.
questions.wrong:
- "RLHF is the proven path, so start there." The full stack is fragile to tune and needs three training loops; the lesson's practical guidance starts with DPO and switches only on a plateau.
- "DPO needs no SFT stage." It needs a reference policy, and that reference is the SFT checkpoint; the single-stage methods are different losses.
- "DPO has no hyperparameters to worry about." Beta decides how far the policy moves from the reference, and the lesson's sweep shows degenerate answers at a small value and no learning at a large one.

questions.title: A DPO trainer whose loss never moves
questions.prompt:
A teammate wrote the core of a DPO trainer. The loss stays at its starting value for the whole run, and the logged margin never moves. Read the code and find what is wrong.

```python
policy = TinyGPT(config)
reference = policy


def sequence_log_prob(model, prompt_ids, completion_ids):
    ids = torch.cat([prompt_ids, completion_ids])
    logits = model(ids[:-1].unsqueeze(0))[0]
    log_probs = logits.log_softmax(-1)
    targets = ids[1:]
    return log_probs[torch.arange(len(targets)), targets].sum()


def dpo_loss(prompt, chosen, rejected, beta=0.1):
    pi_w = sequence_log_prob(policy, prompt, chosen)
    pi_l = sequence_log_prob(policy, prompt, rejected)
    ref_w = sequence_log_prob(reference, prompt, chosen)
    ref_l = sequence_log_prob(reference, prompt, rejected)
    z = beta * ((pi_l - ref_l) - (pi_w - ref_w))
    return -torch.nn.functional.logsigmoid(z)
```
questions.short: Three things. The reference is the same object as the policy, so both log ratios are zero by construction and the loss is a constant with no gradient; build the reference as a separate copy, freeze it, and run it under no gradient. The margin has the wrong sign, so once the aliasing is fixed the trainer promotes the rejected answer. The log-probability also sums over the prompt positions, which the capstone masks out.
questions.full:
### Bug 1: the reference is the policy

`reference = policy` binds a second name to one module. Every forward pass through `reference` uses the current policy weights, so `pi_w - ref_w` and `pi_l - ref_l` are exactly zero, and the loss is a constant. The optimizer sees a zero gradient. A deep copy alone is not enough either: the reference needs `requires_grad=False` on every parameter, its forward passes belong under `torch.no_grad()`, and the policy must start from the same weights, for example with `policy.load_state_dict(reference.state_dict())`.

### Bug 2: the margin has the wrong sign

The loss is minus the log sigmoid of beta times the chosen log ratio minus the rejected log ratio. The code subtracts in the other order. The gradient with respect to the chosen log-probability must be negative, so that raising it lowers the loss. With the reversed sign, the trainer lowers the chosen answer and raises the rejected one. A unit test that checks the gradient sign on one pair catches this.

### Observation 3: the prompt is in the sum

`sequence_log_prob` sums over every position, the prompt included. With one shared prompt, the prompt terms cancel in the margin, so the value is right. But the trainer computes and backpropagates through positions that carry no preference signal, and the cancellation breaks when a long sequence is cut at a maximum length. Start the sum at the first answer position, as the capstone does.

### How to test the fix

- The loss on one pair falls when you raise the chosen log-probability by hand.
- The reference log-probabilities are identical between epochs.
- The mean chosen minus rejected margin under the policy grows over training.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** After the fix, how do you confirm that the reference never moves? Expected: assert that no reference parameter requires a gradient, and compare its log-probabilities on a fixed pair before and after an epoch.
- **Level 3:** Why does every pair start at the same loss before training? Expected: the policy equals the reference, so both log ratios are zero and the sigmoid sits at one half; the margin grows from there.
- **Level 3:** The margin grows, but the generated answers get worse. What do you log next? Expected: the absolute chosen log-probability; DPO can push it down as long as the rejected falls faster.
- **Level 4:** Would you keep the prompt positions if the two answers had different prompts? Expected: no, and the loss would be wrong anyway; the derivation needs one prompt per pair, because the partition term cancels only then.
questions.wrong:
- "Lower the learning rate; the loss is flat because the steps are too small." The gradient is exactly zero while the reference aliases the policy; no step size fixes that.
- "The sign does not matter, the optimizer finds the direction." The sign decides which answer the trainer promotes; reversed, it trains the model to prefer the rejected answers.
- "Replace the sum with a mean to stabilize the loss." That turns the objective into a length-normalized variant; it is a design choice, not the fix for a constant loss.

questions.title: Remove a cause of the gap before you reweight it
questions.prompt: Your RL run shows a steady disagreement between trainer and rollout engine on the probability of each sampled token. One engineer wants to turn on a capped importance weighting right away. Another says it is a kernel artifact and should be ignored. Lay out how you decide, and what you would try first.
questions.short: Match the method to the source of the gap. Five sources exist: tokens re-encoded between turns, expert routing on a mixture model, a sampler that cuts the vocabulary, numeric differences between kernels or precisions, and stale samples. The first three have corrections that remove the cause; try those first, because a reweighting such as truncated importance sampling leaves the gap in place and adds variance to the gradient. A flat gap on a dense model with plain sampling is the kernel floor of that setup; measure it, keep it inside your range, and reweight only what remains after the causes are gone.
questions.full:
### Two kinds of method

A method that removes a cause makes both sides compute the same thing, and that part of the gap is gone. A method that reweights leaves the gap and changes how much each token counts in the loss. Remove causes first.

| Method | Kind | Cause |
|---|---|---|
| Sampling replay | removes | top-p and top-k cut the vocabulary on the engine side only |
| Routing replay | removes | a mixture-of-experts router picks different experts on each side |
| Token-in, token-out sessions | removes | text round trips between agent turns change the tokens |
| True on-policy mode | removes | all kernel differences, for the models and GPUs it covers |
| Truncated importance sampling | reweights | any remaining gap |
| A sample age limit | drops | samples from older weights |

### What the manual measured

Sampling replay on one seed lowered the median gap from 0.0153 to 0.0135, 11.5 percent. No step of the replay run reached the lowest step of the plain run, and the reward stayed in the same range. The sampler part is not noise: a top-p cut raises the engine's log-probability of a kept token by minus the log of the kept mass, which at a top-p of 0.9 was a median shift of about 0.053 in a check outside the training framework. Deterministic inference removed nothing, because it is not a correction.

### The kernel floor

On a dense model in BF16 on both sides, the manual's gap stayed at about 0.015 per token in every healthy run. That is the floor of one setup, not a law. A check with FP16 on both sides cut the median gap about 7.8 times, from 0.0073 to 0.00094 on a serving engine against a reference forward pass, and the worst token fell from 0.355 to 0.033. FP16 on one side only did not help. Precision is a lever that removes a cause, and it costs numeric range.

### When to reweight

Truncated importance sampling weights each token by the ratio of the trainer probability to the engine probability and caps the ratio, with `--use-tis --tis-clip 2.0` as the manual's example. Use it for a gap you cannot remove: a low-precision rollout, where FP8 rounding has no kernel fix, or a mixture model after routing replay. Pair it with the step-0 check, so that the reweighting never hides a setup error.

### How to run the comparison

Same seed, same steps, one change per run, and the gap read at every step. A method that helps shows a lower gap on the same steps. A gap that grows after a change names the cause you added.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** Why does a reweighting add variance? Expected: tokens with a large ratio get a large weight, so a few tokens dominate the update; the cap limits that, but does not remove it.
- **Level 3:** Replay needs both a top-k and a top-p set. Why is the top-k needed? Expected: the framework requires a positive top-k for replay, so a run with top-p alone changes the sampler without replaying the kept set.
- **Level 4:** FP16 on the engine and BF16 on the trainer did not close the gap. Why? Expected: each side's own rounding sets a floor; the gap closes only when both sides round the same way, so the precision must match on both sides.
- **Level 4:** When is the bit-exact mode the right answer, and when is it not available? Expected: when you need a gap of zero and your model and GPU are in its contract; it pins one attention kernel and batch-invariant operations for specific dense models on one GPU generation, and refuses the rest.
questions.wrong:
- "Turn on importance sampling first; it is cheap." It leaves every cause in place, adds variance, and hides a setup error that the step-0 check would show.
- "The gap is a kernel artifact, so it never matters." The sampler part was measurable and removable, and a gap that grows after a change is a cause you added.
- "Deterministic inference is a correction method." It makes the engine repeat itself and leaves the gap where it was; the manual's four runs show the same gap with it on and off.

questions.title: A flat GRPO reward and the groups that teach nothing
questions.prompt: A GRPO run trains a small model on grade-school math with a binary reward. The reward per step jumps around, and the trend over many steps looks flat. The team wants to raise the learning rate. What do you read first, and what do you suspect?
questions.short: Read the group statistics before you touch the learning rate. GRPO scores each answer against the mean of its group, so a group where every answer is right or every answer is wrong has a zero advantage for every member and teaches nothing. In the manual's runs, 10 of the 32 groups in the first step had one reward for all 8 answers, and about half of the groups did over 12 steps. If most groups are like that, the signal is thin, and the fix is the prompt mix or the dynamic sampling filter, not a bigger step.
questions.full:
### Read five numbers, not the reward

The reward of one step moved by up to 0.14 between steps in the first ten steps of the manual's runs, and by up to 0.21 over a long run, so read a mean over five or more steps. Next to it read the answer length, the share of answers cut at the length limit, the log-probability gap between the trainer and the engine, and the KL between them. A flat reward with a flat gap and a normal length points at the signal, not at the kernels.

### Count the groups that carry no advantage

The rollout `perf` line counts groups with a zero standard deviation: `rollout/zero_std/count_1` for all right and `rollout/zero_std/count_0` for all wrong. In the first step of the manual's baseline, 7 groups were all right and 3 were all wrong, 10 of 32. Over 12 steps with one seed, 191 of 384 groups had one reward for every answer, and 142 of those were all right: easy prompts the model already solved.

### The filter and its cost

The dynamic sampling filter drops those groups and asks the engine for more prompts until the step holds enough groups with a spread. With batches of 48 prompts for 32 kept groups, the manual's steps dropped 16 to 48 groups each, median 36, and most dropped groups were all right. The rollout took 1.5 times as long when one extra batch was enough and 2.8 times as long when a second batch was needed. The sum of the twelve step times went from 60 minutes to 113.

### Read the reward with the filter on

`rollout/raw_reward` no longer includes the dropped groups, so compare `rollout/raw_reward_unfiltered` instead. Even that number leaned high in the manual's run, 0.686 against 0.657, because the slowest and longest answers were stopped before they counted, and a cut answer usually scores 0. Treat a gain inside the spread of your baseline seeds as noise.

### What a higher learning rate would do

A larger step on a thin signal raises the gradient norm and the variance of the update without adding information. The manual's rule for a gradient norm that grows step after step is the opposite: lower the rate.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** Why does a group with one reward give a zero advantage? Expected: GRPO subtracts the group mean and divides by the group standard deviation; equal rewards give a zero numerator for every answer.
- **Level 2:** What else makes a math reward score 0 besides a wrong answer? Expected: an answer cut at the length limit before its final line; read the cut share next to the reward.
- **Level 3:** The filter run shows a higher mean reward than the baseline. How do you decide if it learned more? Expected: compare the unfiltered reward, account for the bias from stopped long answers, and run a second seed against the spread of the baseline seeds.
- **Level 3:** Your reward returns fractions, and a group with identical rewards still shows small nonzero advantages. Why? Expected: float32 rounding of the group mean leaves a remainder that the division by a near-zero standard deviation blows up; round rewards to values a float32 holds exactly.
questions.wrong:
- "Raise the learning rate; the reward is flat because the steps are small." The signal is thin because many groups carry no advantage; a larger step amplifies noise and raises the gradient norm.
- "Sample more answers per prompt to get a spread." In the manual's runs, 4, 8 and 16 answers per prompt gave reward gains inside one seed range, and more answers made each rollout longer.
- "Read the reward of the last step." One step moves by up to a fifth of the scale; read the mean over five or more steps.

questions.title: What the KL penalty in RLHF protects
questions.prompt: In the PPO stage of RLHF, the objective subtracts a KL term between the policy and a frozen copy of the SFT model. A new hire asks why the pipeline keeps a second copy of the model in memory for that one term. Explain the failure it prevents and how you tune its coefficient.
questions.short: The reward model was trained on answers that look like SFT output. Without the term, PPO moves the policy into regions the reward model never saw and finds strings that score high but that people dislike. The term charges the policy for leaving the SFT distribution, so it is a regularizer, not a hard constraint. Tune beta from the measured KL: too low and the reward climbs together with the KL, too high and the policy barely moves from SFT.
questions.full:
### The objective

```text
maximize  E[ R(x, y) ]  -  beta * KL( policy(. | x) || reference(. | x) )
```

The reference is the SFT checkpoint, frozen. The reward model scores whole answers; the KL is summed over the tokens of each answer and subtracted from the reward.

### Without the KL term

The reward model is a finite fit to human preferences and has blind spots. Repeated phrases that signal helpfulness, verbose formal text with no content, bullet points everywhere: each scored high in real pipelines. With no anchor the policy collapses toward a few high-reward modes. The toy three-stage pipeline in the InstructGPT lesson shows this inside 50 update steps when beta is 0.

### Reading the KL

Track the mean KL per answer on every update. The lesson on reward modeling gives 5 to 10 nats, summed over tokens, as the point where the policy has drifted far from SFT: either beta is too low, or reward hacking has started.

### Tuning beta

Reference values: 0.01 to 0.05 in the lesson on reward modeling, 0.02 in the pipeline that the RLHF lesson describes. The common trick is an adaptive beta with a target KL. When the observed KL passes the target, beta doubles; when it falls under half the target, beta halves. The library the lesson shows uses a target of 6.0 with the adaptive controller on.

### The second anchor

The KL protects style and distribution. It does not protect benchmark skill that the reward never asks for. That drop is the alignment tax, and the fix mixes pretraining gradients into the RL objective.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** Why is the term a regularizer and not a trust region? Expected: it adds a cost that grows with the distance; nothing stops the policy from paying it, so a large reward can still buy a large move.
- **Level 2:** What two things must be true of the reference model in code? Expected: its weights never receive gradients, and it never shares parameters with the policy; a shared module silently removes the anchor.
- **Level 3:** The reward rises, the KL rises, and human ratings stay flat. Which knob first? Expected: raise beta or stop early; then widen the reward model's training data so that the exploited region is covered.
- **Level 3:** After RLHF the model scores lower on reading comprehension benchmarks. Is that the KL's job? Expected: no; that is the alignment tax, addressed by a pretraining log-likelihood term in the objective, as the PPO-ptx variant does.
questions.wrong:
- "Drop the reference model to save memory and clip the PPO ratio harder." The clip bounds one update; it does not bound the drift over many updates, which is what the KL does.
- "Set beta high to be safe." A high beta pins the policy to SFT, and the run buys nothing for its compute.
- "KL is a safety filter for harmful text." It measures distance from the SFT distribution and knows nothing about content; a safe reference is what makes it useful.

questions.title: A step-0 gap several times the healthy range
questions.prompt: You start a GRPO run with a new model checkpoint. At step 0, the metric that compares the trainer's log-probabilities with the rollout engine's reads several times higher than on your earlier runs with the same model family. A colleague suggests turning on the engine's deterministic mode to close it. What do you do?
questions.short: Stop the run before it trains on wrong numbers. At step 0 both sides hold the same weights, so a value far above your healthy range means the two sides do not compute the same model: a wrong checkpoint path on one side, or a format that one side reads differently. Deterministic inference does not help; in the manual's runs it left the gap unchanged at about 0.015 and made the engine repeat itself, which is a different property. Fix the setup, then compare the step-0 value with the range of your healthy runs.
questions.full:
### What step 0 proves

No training has happened yet. The trainer scores the sampled tokens with the weights the engine used, so every difference comes from the setup. Two values must be exactly 0 at step 0: `train/ppo_kl`, the KL between the trainer's old and new probabilities, and `train/pg_clipfrac`, the share of clipped tokens. The gap itself, `train/train_rollout_logprob_abs_diff`, is never 0 outside the bit-exact mode, because the two sides run different kernels. It must still sit inside your range.

### The ranges in the manual

| Setup | Gap at step 0 |
|---|---|
| Qwen3-0.6B, plain sampling, 17 runs | 0.0148 to 0.0157 |
| Qwen3-0.6B, top-p 0.95 and top-k 64 | 0.0136 |
| Qwen3-1.7B | 0.0109 |

The gap depends on the model and the sampler, so build the range from your own seeds. A value several times the range points at the model, not at the kernels.

### Why deterministic mode is the wrong tool

Deterministic inference makes the engine give the same result for a request, whatever the batch around it. In four 12-step runs with one seed, the median gap was 0.01526 with the default engine and 0.01518, 0.01520 and 0.01515 with deterministic kernels on two attention backends. Two deterministic runs repeated the step-0 gap to six decimal places, 0.015404. So the mode buys repeatability, not agreement, and it cost 40 to 45 percent more rollout time on clean steps.

### The checks, in order

1. The checkpoint paths of both sides. With the trainer the manual uses, both sides load from one argument; a split layout or a low-precision engine loads two files, and they must hold the same model.
2. The model format: a conversion step that one side applies and the other does not.
3. The weight equality check on a two-step run after the first update, with the quantization tolerance on when the engine runs in low precision.
4. The sampler. A top-p or top-k setting on one run and not on the other moves the gap, as the table shows.

### What a healthy gap does over a run

It stays flat. In the manual's three baseline seeds, every step over 48 steps stayed between 0.0136 and 0.0164, and the KL between the two sides stayed between 0.00063 and 0.00076. A gap that jumps and stays high after a weight update means the two sides no longer hold the same weights.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** Why is the gap never zero in a normal run? Expected: the two sides add the same numbers in a different order, with different kernels; across many layers and a large vocabulary the rounding adds up.
- **Level 3:** What does the deterministic mode buy, then? Expected: the same rollout for the same seed, which is what you need to test a reward function on identical samples.
- **Level 4:** Which levers move the floor of the gap itself? Expected: the precision on both sides, the tensor-parallel size of the engine, and kernels that add in one fixed order; each costs speed or work.
- **Level 4:** The gap is fine at step 0 and grows step after step. What is different from the step-0 failure? Expected: the weights diverge after updates, so the weight update path is the suspect, not the checkpoint; read the update logs and run the weight equality check.
questions.wrong:
- "Turn on deterministic inference to close the gap." The manual's four runs show the same gap with and without it; it makes the engine repeat itself and costs rollout time.
- "A gap is normal; keep training and watch the reward." A step-0 value several times the healthy range means the trainer scores a different model than the one that sampled, so the run trains on wrong numbers from the first update.
- "Add an importance-sampling correction." A reweighting hides a gap that comes from a setup error; remove the cause first.

questions.title: Count the parameters of one LoRA adapter
questions.prompt: An attention projection in your model is a square matrix with 4,096 rows and 4,096 columns. You add a LoRA adapter of rank 16 to it. How many values does the adapter train, and what share of the frozen matrix is that? Then say what changes when you double the rank.
questions.short: The adapter is two thin matrices: A with 16 rows and 4,096 columns, and B with 4,096 rows and 16 columns. Each holds 65,536 values, so the adapter trains 131,072 parameters. The frozen matrix holds 16,777,216, so the adapter is 0.78 percent of it. A doubled rank doubles the adapter, because its size is linear in the rank.
questions.full:
### The count

```text
y = W x + (alpha / r) B A x
A: r x d_in  = 16 x 4096 = 65,536
B: d_out x r = 4096 x 16 = 65,536
adapter      = 131,072
W            = 4096 x 4096 = 16,777,216
share        = 0.78 percent
```

### Why so few parameters work

The update that fine-tuning makes to a weight matrix has a low intrinsic rank. A rank of 16 or 32 captures most of it. The lesson reports LoRA at rank 16 within about one point of full fine-tuning on the benchmarks it lists.

### The rank table

| Rank | Parameters for one 4096 by 4096 matrix |
|---|---|
| 4 | 32,768 |
| 8 | 65,536 |
| 16 | 131,072 |
| 32 | 262,144 |
| 64 | 524,288 |

### Alpha

The scale `alpha / r` sets how much the adapter output counts. With alpha equal to the rank, the scale is one; a common convention sets alpha to twice the rank. Alpha changes the effective step size, not the parameter count.

### Which matrices

The count above is one matrix. Adapters on the query and value projections of every layer are the usual start. Adding the key and output projections and the MLP layers raises quality a little and, on the lesson's 7B table, raises the count from 9.4M to 37.7M.
questions.followups:
- **Level 1:** Why does B start at zero? Expected: the product B A is then zero, so the model starts from its original behavior and learns the change step by step.
- **Level 2:** How does the count change for a matrix that is not square? Expected: A is r by the input width and B is the output height by r, so the count is r times the sum of the two sides; still linear in the rank.
- **Level 2:** At what rank does the memory advantage start to fade? Expected: the lesson puts the point of diminishing returns past 64, where quality stops improving and the adapters stop being small.
- **Level 3:** After training, how do you remove the cost of the second matrix product at inference? Expected: merge, compute W plus alpha over r times B A once, and save a full matrix of the original size.
questions.wrong:
- "The adapter trains r squared parameters." It trains r times the sum of the two matrix sides; r squared would be a tiny block, not the two thin matrices.
- "Doubling the rank doubles the quality." The gain flattens fast; the lesson finds rank 16 within about one point of full fine-tuning and little gain past 64.
- "Alpha adds parameters." Alpha is a fixed scalar on the adapter output; it changes the effective step size, not the count.

questions.title: Plan the post-training of a support assistant
questions.prompt: Take-home. A company wants a support assistant built from an open 8B base model. They have about 50,000 past support conversations with customer ratings, two 24 GB GPUs, and three weeks. Write the post-training plan on one page: the stages, the data for each stage, the settings you start from, what you measure after each stage, and the three failure modes you guard against.
questions.short: Three stages: first, SFT with QLoRA on the top-rated conversations in one chat template with the loss masked to the assistant turns, at a low learning rate for one to three epochs with a few percent of raw text mixed in, measured by held-out instruction loss, raw-text drift and a sample read. Second, DPO against the SFT checkpoint as the frozen reference, on pairs built from high- and low-rated answers to the same prompt with a conservative beta, measured by a blind pairwise eval and the absolute chosen log-probability, not the training margin. Third, a release gate: a fixed prompt set rated blind, a refusal set, and a comparison with the base model on tasks the data never covered. The guards are catastrophic forgetting, length and agreement exploits in the ratings, and over-optimization of the preference proxy.
questions.full:
### Stage 0: data

- Convert every conversation into one chat template, with a fixed system prompt.
- SFT set: the top-rated answers, filtered for length, vocabulary diversity and a clean instruction-to-answer ratio. Tens of thousands of clean examples are enough; the reference SFT stage in the lesson used about 27,000.
- Preference set: for prompts with both a high-rated and a low-rated answer, build prompt, chosen and rejected triples. Where the data is thin, sample the rejected side from the SFT model, so that the pairs are in-distribution for the reference. A rater or a judge must confirm that each sampled answer is worse than the chosen one before it becomes a pair, because the SFT model trained on top-rated answers and its samples can be as good. Aim for the 5,000 to 20,000 pairs where DPO works well.
- A blind eval set of prompts never used in training, plus a forgetting set of tasks outside support, such as short code and arithmetic.

### Stage 1: SFT with QLoRA

Two 24 GB cards cannot hold a full update of this model; a 7B full update needs about 56 GB with gradients and optimizer states. QLoRA keeps the base in 4-bit and trains adapters of rank 16 on the attention projections in about 6 GB, so each card runs its own experiment.

Start from: the lesson's SFT learning rate of 2e-5 for a full update, with a higher rate for adapters as the LoRA lesson's trainer shows; one to three epochs; 2 to 5 percent raw pretraining text mixed into the batches.

Measure: held-out instruction loss, raw-text loss before and after with a budget of a 10 to 15 percent rise, exact match on the templated tasks where it applies, and a read of fifty samples.

### Stage 2: DPO

Reference: the merged SFT checkpoint, frozen. Policy: a copy with fresh adapters. Beta in the 0.1 to 0.3 range, a few epochs, and the four log-probabilities per pair over the answer tokens only.

Measure: a blind pairwise eval against the SFT model on the held-out prompts, the implicit reward margin, the absolute chosen log-probability, the response length by checkpoint, and the forgetting set again. Stop on the eval, not on the margin.

### Stage 3: release gate

- A fixed prompt set rated blind by people, against the SFT checkpoint and the base.
- A refusal and safety set with the expected behavior written down.
- The forgetting set.
- Adapters kept separate for a rollback; a merge only for the shipped artifact.

### The three guards

1. Catastrophic forgetting: low rate, short training, a pretraining mix, and a raw-text loss budget.
2. Exploits of the rating signal: raters liked long and agreeable answers, so watch the length and the agreement with the premise, and filter pairs where length alone separates them.
3. Over-optimization of the proxy: the DPO ratio can be pushed off the data, so stop early on the blind eval and keep beta conservative.

### Schedule

Week one: data and SFT. Week two: DPO and the first blind eval. Week three: the gate, a second seed of the best configuration, and the rollback plan.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** Why DPO and not a reward model with PPO here? Expected: tens of thousands of pairs, two small GPUs and three weeks fit the DPO regime; a reward model and PPO need three loops and more memory.
- **Level 4:** The ratings are one to five stars on single answers, not pairs. What changes? Expected: build pairs only where one prompt has answers at both ends of the scale, or use the unpaired loss that works on good and bad labels and keep the pairs for the eval.
- **Level 4:** How do you prove that the DPO stage did not degrade the SFT behavior? Expected: the blind pairwise eval against the SFT checkpoint, the forgetting set, and the absolute chosen log-probability; a margin that grows while those fall is a stop signal.
- **Level 4:** What would make you add an RL stage with a verifier? Expected: a part of the task with a checkable answer, such as a correct order number or a passing code snippet, where a binary reward and group-relative advantages give a signal the ratings do not.
questions.wrong:
- "Skip SFT and run DPO on the base model." DPO needs a reference that already follows instructions; the single-stage loss is a different method, and the base model's pairs are out of distribution.
- "Fully fine-tune the 8B model across both GPUs." A full update of a model this size needs about 56 GB with the optimizer states; two 24 GB cards hold it only with adapters and a 4-bit base.
- "Use the star ratings as the reward and run PPO." A regression on absolute scores is the weak label the lessons warn about, and the full stack does not fit the compute or the timeline.

questions.title: Pick a preference loss for four kinds of data
questions.prompt: Four teams bring you four datasets. One has thumbs-up and thumbs-down clicks on single answers. One has paired comparisons whose preferred answers are mostly twice the length of the rejected ones. One has no SFT checkpoint and wants a single training stage from the base model. One has pairs where some preferences are near coin flips and others are unanimous. Which preference loss do you recommend to each team, and why?
questions.short: The clicks team gets the prospect-theory loss that works on single labels. The length-skewed team gets the reference-free loss that normalizes by length and adds a margin, so a longer winner does not win by its token count. The team without an SFT stage gets the odds-ratio loss, which adds a preference term to the SFT likelihood and trains from the base in one pass; the team with mixed preference strengths gets the identity-mapping loss, whose margin is bounded. Each one repairs one assumption that plain DPO makes.
questions.full:
### Start from what DPO assumes

The DPO derivation assumes paired data, an SFT reference that is the true anchor, in-distribution pairs, and a preference that maps to an unbounded log-odds. Each member of the family drops or repairs one of these.

| Data or constraint | Loss | What it changes |
|---|---|---|
| Single answers with good or bad labels | KTO | prospect-theory utility on one label; losses weigh more than gains; no pairs needed |
| Winners much longer than losers | SimPO | average log-probability per token plus a margin; no reference model |
| No SFT checkpoint, one stage | ORPO | SFT negative log-likelihood plus an odds-ratio preference term; the SFT term is the regularizer |
| Preference strength varies widely | IPO | squared error on a target of one over two beta; the gap is bounded |
| Chosen log-probability falls in the DPO logs | BPO | DPO plus a penalty on downward moves of the chosen answer |
| A large clean paired set | DPO | a conservative beta |

### The reasoning for each team

1. Clicks are plentiful and unpaired. Forcing them into pairs throws away most of the data; the unpaired loss uses every label.
2. In plain DPO a long winner has a more negative log-probability by construction, so the gap grows for the wrong reason and the policy learns length. Normalizing by length removes the incentive. Without a reference, drift needs a guard of its own.
3. The single-stage loss trains the base model to follow instructions and to prefer the chosen answer at once; the likelihood term keeps it anchored where DPO used the reference.
4. In DPO a near coin-flip pair and a unanimous pair both push toward an unbounded gap. The bounded loss keeps the gap proportional to the preference strength.

### What every team keeps

A held-out eval with generation, early stopping, and a check on the absolute chosen log-probability. None of these losses escapes over-optimization; they move where it bites.

### How to decide in practice

Run the candidates on one battery and pick per task. The lesson's point is that the best loss for math reasoning has no reason to be the best loss for safety.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** The clicks team also has a small paired set. Combine them? Expected: yes; train with the unpaired loss on the clicks and validate on the pairs, or weight the two losses; the pairs are the cleaner signal for the eval.
- **Level 3:** Why does removing the reference save memory, and what does it cost? Expected: one model in memory instead of two; the cost is no anchor, so the policy can drift, and the margin term and early stopping carry that job.
- **Level 4:** A team runs DPO and watches the probability of its chosen answers drop while the margin grows. Which row applies, and why is it not a tuning problem? Expected: the chosen-preserving variant; the gradient of plain DPO cares only about the difference, so no beta fixes the direction.
- **Level 4:** How do you argue to a skeptic that these losses still over-optimize? Expected: the published curves of gold reward against KL for direct methods show the same peak and collapse as reward-model pipelines; the implicit reward queries out-of-distribution samples, and KL regularization does not stabilize it.
questions.wrong:
- "Convert the clicks into pairs by matching a good and a bad answer for the same prompt." It keeps only prompts with both labels and invents comparisons the raters never made; the unpaired loss uses the labels as they are.
- "Truncate the long winners so that the pairs are balanced." That destroys the answers people preferred; the fix is in the loss normalization, not in the data.
- "Use DPO everywhere and tune beta per team." Beta cannot create pairs, remove a reference, bound a gap or supply an SFT stage; each of those is a different loss.

questions.title: Fit a 7B fine-tune on a 24 GB GPU
questions.prompt: You have one GPU with 24 GB of memory and want to fine-tune a 7B model on your own instruction data. Walk me through the memory for a full update, for LoRA and for QLoRA, and say what makes the last one fit.
questions.short: A full update of a 7B model needs about 56 GB: the weights in half precision, the gradients, and two optimizer states per parameter, all in half precision. LoRA keeps the half-precision weights but trains only small adapters, so the gradients and optimizer states shrink and the run takes about 18 GB. QLoRA stores the frozen base in 4-bit, about 3.5 GB of weights, and trains the adapters in half precision, so the run takes about 6 GB and leaves room for activations on a 24 GB card.
questions.full:
### The memory table

| Method | Weights | Training total | Fits on |
|---|---|---|---|
| Full update, FP16 | 14 GB | about 56 GB before activations, which depend on the workload | one 80 GB datacenter GPU |
| LoRA on an FP16 base | 14 GB | about 18 GB | one 40 GB GPU |
| QLoRA, 4-bit base | 3.5 GB | about 6 GB | one 24 GB consumer GPU |

The 56 GB comes from two bytes per weight, two bytes per gradient, and two optimizer states per parameter; activations come on top of that. This estimate keeps the optimizer states in half precision too. Standard Adam keeps its states in FP32, so a typical full update needs more memory than this, not less. The adapters remove the gradients and the states for every frozen weight, which is the large part.

### What QLoRA adds

1. NF4. A 4-bit type whose 16 levels sit at the quantiles of a normal distribution, which matches how weights are distributed and loses less than uniform 4-bit integers.
2. Double quantization. Each block of 64 weights needs a scale in FP32, about 0.4 GB for a 7B model; quantizing the scales to 8 bits brings that down to about 0.1 GB.
3. Paged optimizers. Optimizer states page to CPU memory when the GPU runs out, which trades some throughput for no out-of-memory crash from optimizer states. Activations stay on the GPU, so a long sequence can still run out of memory.

### What it costs in quality

The lesson's table puts LoRA at rank 16 within about one point of a full update, QLoRA at rank 16 a fraction behind that, and QLoRA at rank 64 level with the full update on the listed benchmarks.

### What it costs in time and money

On the lesson's cost table, QLoRA at rank 16 on a 24 GB consumer card took about 6 hours and about 5 dollars for 50,000 examples over three epochs. The full update took about 8 hours on two 80 GB datacenter GPUs and about 32 dollars. Fused kernels cut the QLoRA run to about 2.5 hours.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** Why does LoRA cut training memory so much more than it cuts weight memory? Expected: the gradients and the two optimizer states exist only for the adapter parameters, which are a fraction of a percent of the model.
- **Level 2:** The adapters train in half precision while the base is 4-bit. Where does the forward pass compute? Expected: the base weights are dequantized block by block to the compute dtype for each matrix product, and the adapter path runs in half precision.
- **Level 3:** When would you still pay for the full update? Expected: when the task needs changes that a low-rank update cannot express, when you have the data and the GPUs, or when the eval shows a gap that a higher rank does not close.
- **Level 3:** How do you serve several QLoRA fine-tunes from one base? Expected: keep the adapters separate and load them on top of one base copy; merge only when you ship a single specialized model.
questions.wrong:
- "Quantize the whole model to 4-bit and fine-tune it directly." Gradients and optimizer states still need higher precision; the base stays frozen in 4-bit, and only the adapters train.
- "QLoRA halves the quality." The lesson's table shows a loss of a fraction of a point at rank 16 and parity at rank 64.
- "Load the base in 8-bit with LoRA; it is the same thing." Eight-bit weights take twice the memory of NF4, and the double quantization and paged optimizers are what make the 6 GB figure.

questions.title: Why reward models learn from pairs, not scores
questions.prompt: You need a reward model for a helpfulness objective. A product manager suggests asking raters to score each answer from one to ten and regressing on the scores. Why do most pipelines collect pairwise comparisons instead, and what loss do you train with?
questions.short: People are poor at absolute scores and good at relative judgments, so pipelines show two answers to one prompt and ask which is better. The reward model is the SFT model with its vocabulary head replaced by a scalar head. It trains with the Bradley-Terry loss, the negative log of the sigmoid of the reward difference between the preferred and the rejected answer. The difference in reward becomes a log-odds of preference, which turns many relative judgments into one consistent scale.
questions.full:
### The loss

```text
loss = -log( sigmoid( r(x, y_preferred) - r(x, y_rejected) ) )
```

The sigmoid of the difference is the probability that the preferred answer wins. Training pushes the preferred reward up and the rejected reward down. The model reads the hidden state at the last position, because causal attention has seen the whole prompt and answer there, and projects it to one number.

### What accuracy to expect

A random reward model ranks half of the pairs right. The reference pipeline in the RLHF lesson trained its reward model on 33,000 comparisons from 40 raters, about 5 minutes each, and reached about 72 percent accuracy on held-out pairs. That sounds low, but the raters agreed with each other about 73 percent of the time. That agreement estimates the noise in the labels. It is not a hard bound, but a score far above it is a reason to look for a leak.

### Noise in the labels

Roughly 30 percent of human labels are noisy or ambiguous. Filter pairs by rater agreement, or add a temperature to the sigmoid. Pairs where both answers are bad still teach the model which one is less bad.

### Size

A reward model that is too small cannot score the policy's outputs faithfully. The lesson's table lists a 6B reward model for a 175B policy in one pipeline, and a 52B reward model trained on 22,000 comparisons in another. Larger reward models gave more stable signals to the RL stage.

### Where the reward model lives later

The same scalar head powers best-of-N sampling at decode time and the reward side of reasoning pipelines. It is the entry to the whole alignment stack.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** Why read the last token's hidden state and not a mean over positions? Expected: with a causal mask the last position has attended to the whole sequence, so it holds the most complete summary; mean pooling is an alternative worth a test.
- **Level 2:** Your reward model ranks 90 percent of the test pairs right. Good news? Expected: suspicious; with rater agreement near 73 percent, that score suggests a leak or a shortcut such as length, so check what the model keys on.
- **Level 3:** How do you turn comparisons into a reward for several criteria at once? Expected: one reward model per criterion, such as helpfulness and safety, combined with weights; a single model learns a blur of the criteria.
- **Level 4:** Why does the reward model need protection from the policy later? Expected: it saw only in-distribution answers; a policy under optimization moves off that distribution and finds answers that score high for the wrong reasons, which is why the RL stage carries a KL penalty.
questions.wrong:
- "Regress on a one-to-ten score; it is more information per label." Absolute scores drift between raters and sessions; a pairwise judgment is cheap and consistent, and the Bradley-Terry fit recovers a scale from it.
- "72 percent accuracy means the reward model is broken." The raters agreed only about 73 percent of the time; the model is near the agreement of its labels.
- "Use a small reward model to save compute." A reward model that cannot represent the policy's outputs gives a noisy signal, and the policy exploits its blind spots.

questions.title: The reward climbs and the human ratings do not
questions.prompt: Four days into a PPO run, the mean score from the reward model keeps climbing. A blind human rating of samples from each checkpoint is flat, and the last two checkpoints read slightly worse. The team wants to keep training because the curve looks great. What do you say?
questions.short: Stop, and treat it as reward hacking. The policy has found outputs that the reward model scores high but people do not prefer, because the reward model is a finite proxy with blind spots. Read the KL to the reference and the length and format of recent samples; a KL that climbs with the reward and answers that grow longer or more formulaic confirm it. Roll back to the checkpoint where the human rating peaked, raise the KL coefficient or stop earlier, and widen the reward model's training data to cover what the policy exploited.
questions.full:
### The signature

Reward up, human eval flat or down. The reward model was trained on in-distribution answers; the policy under optimization leaves that distribution and the reward model extrapolates. The RLHF lesson's table of what real pipelines saw:

| Failure | What the samples show | Why the reward model liked it |
|---|---|---|
| Verbosity | longer and longer answers | raters preferred detail, so the model learned length |
| Sycophancy | agreement with the user's premise | agreeable answers were rated higher |
| Hedging | no commitment to an answer | hedged answers are rarely marked wrong |
| Format gaming | headers and bullets everywhere | formatted answers looked polished |

### The checks

1. The mean KL to the reference per answer. The warning line in the lesson on reward modeling is 5 to 10 nats summed over tokens; past it, the policy has drifted far from SFT.
2. The response length by checkpoint. Length hacking is the most common form.
3. Fifty samples read side by side across checkpoints. The failure modes above are visible to the eye.
4. The blind human eval you already have. Keep it blind and held out; it is the one measure the policy cannot game.

### The fixes

- Roll back to the best checkpoint by human rating; the reward curve is not the objective.
- Raise beta, or use an adaptive beta with a target KL, so that the policy pays more to leave the reference.
- Normalize the reward for length, or add a length-aware term.
- Add the exploited answers, rated by people, to the reward model's data, retrain it, and continue from the rollback.
- Train more than one reward model on different data; one exploit rarely fits all of them.

### Why the curve is not the goal

The reward model is a statistical proxy for a sample of human rankings, not for human values. Optimizing a proxy hard enough finds its errors. Every alignment pipeline since has carried a blind human eval for that reason.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** How do you tell reward hacking from a reward model that is right and raters who are wrong? Expected: read the samples; if people consistently dislike what scores high, the proxy is wrong, because the raters define the objective.
- **Level 3:** The reward model is small to save compute. Does that matter here? Expected: yes; a reward model that cannot represent the policy's outputs has more blind spots, and the lessons warn against one smaller than the policy.
- **Level 4:** You switch to DPO to get rid of the reward model. Does the problem go away? Expected: no; the implicit reward can be over-optimized the same way, with the same peak-and-collapse curve, so the blind eval and early stopping stay.
- **Level 4:** Design a guard that stops a run on its own. Expected: a held-out human or trusted-judge eval on a fixed prompt set at each checkpoint, a KL budget, and a stop rule for an eval that falls while the reward rises.
questions.wrong:
- "The human raters are noisy; trust the reward model." The reward model was fit to those raters; when they disagree with it on new samples, the model is extrapolating wrong.
- "Lower beta so the policy can find even better answers." A lower beta lets the policy move further from the distribution the reward model knows, which is the cause of the problem.
- "Keep training; the human eval will catch up." The lessons describe a plateau or a decline in human ratings while the reward climbs; more steps make the exploit stronger.

questions.title: Write and prove a custom reward for GRPO
questions.prompt: Take-home. The RL framework you use scores each sampled answer with a reward function that you swap in by import path. Write a reward for a task with a numeric final answer, write a test plan for it, and explain how you would prove that your reward does not break the GRPO advantages before a long run. Keep the function and the plan short enough to read in five minutes.
